short: The name Batavi is derived from the Germanic tribe of Batavi, who lived in the lower reaches of the Rhine and the Maas. Roman authors described the Batavians as valiant and brave warriors. In 12 B.C. Drusus the Elder concluded an alliance with them, which obliged the Batavians to provide soldiers for military service to the Romans. Votive inscription from Hungary (Brigetio – Komárom (Pannonia superior), from a stone now known as the Altar of Jupiter), mentioning a T BAT has been expanded to «t(ribunus) Bat(avorum)», and is dated to 303. If the identification is correct, it shows the original Batavi auxilia palatina unit, like the Cornuti, was one of the first of the auxilia palatina to be raised. When the unit was split between seniores and iuniores, is not known for certain. In the 50s of the 4th centuries, the Batavi were among the troops of the Gallic army, fighting under the command of Caesar Julian in the wars with the Alemanni and other Germanic tribes. In 357, the Batavi occupied the right flank of the second line of the Roman battle order at the Battle of Argentoratum. They came to aid the Cornuti and Brachiati, who had taken the Germanic cavalry attack. Ammianus mentions the Batavi standing in reserve during the battle of Adrianople. It is possible that if the Batavi had joined the fight in time, the battle's fate would have been different. However, when Magister Victor rushed to them in order to bring them to help, he could not find them: the Batavi preferred not to tempt fate and took care of their own survival.
history: One of the simplest forms of one-armed catapult, the onager relied on twisted skeins of animal sinew which provided the power to hurl either rocks or shot. Inaccurate but powerful, it was an effective siege machine against buildings and fortifications, but was of far less use on the battlefield unless firing into massed infantry ranks. First mentioned by Philon of Byzantium in his treatise on ‘Mechanics’, the onager made use of a sling-like cradle attached to a firing arm. This arm was inserted, twisted, and propelled rocks or shot through torsion. As the firing arm was released, the sling-like cradle would unhook, firing the projectile. A padded beam was incorporated into the housing frame to restrain the arm. Larger machines could require as many as eight or ten crewmen, and the incredible recoil meant that they could not be easily or safely mounted on walls or towers. Quickly constructed wherever wood was readily available, onagers soon became a staple of ancient siege warfare.
strengths: Very low damage and armour penetration
